patient.chief_complaint: Severe headache, fever, and confusion over 12 hours
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darnell Washington is a 45-year-old right-handed man and high school basketball coach who was brought to the emergency department by his wife at approximately 06:15 this morning. His wife reports that he came home from practice yesterday afternoon complaining of a progressively worsening headache that he initially attributed to a sinus flare-up, given his chronic sinusitis history. He took 800 mg of ibuprofen and went to bed early at around 20:00. She checked on him at 23:00 and noted he felt warm to the touch and was sweating profusely. She took his temperature with a home thermometer and recorded 38.9 degrees Celsius. She gave him 1000 mg of acetaminophen and encouraged fluids. Overnight, he became progressively more confused and agitated, calling out names she did not recognize and not responding appropriately to her questions. By 05:30 this morning, she found him curled in the fetal position in bed, moaning, with his hands covering his eyes. He complained that the bedroom light was unbearable and that his neck felt stiff and painful. He vomited twice. He was unable to stand without assistance. On arrival to the ED, his temperature was 39.7 degrees Celsius. He was tachycardic and appeared acutely ill, diaphoretic, and photophobic. He could state his name but was unable to provide any further history. His wife denies any recent travel, sick contacts with meningitis, or known immunocompromised state, though she notes he has been more tired than usual over the past week and had nasal congestion he attributed to allergies. She confirms his vaccinations are up to date for his age but is unsure about meningococcal vaccination. There is no history of head trauma, seizure activity, or new rash.

output.query: bacterial meningitis empiric treatment guidelines adults 2024

results.title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis
results.authors: Tunkel AR, Hartman BJ, Kaplan SL, et al.
results.key_finding: Empiric therapy for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults aged 18-50: vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h or cefotaxime 2g IV q4-6h). Add ampicillin if age >50 or immunocompromised for Listeria coverage.

results.title: Adjunctive Dexamethasone in Bacterial Meningitis
results.authors: de Gans J, van de Beek D.
results.key_finding: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV q6h for 4 days, started before or with the first dose of antibiotics, significantly reduced unfavorable outcomes and mortality in adults with pneumococcal meningitis.

results.title: Community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults: updated ESCMID guidelines
results.authors: van de Beek D, Cabellos C, Dezure A, et al.
results.key_finding: Duration of therapy for pneumococcal meningitis: 10-14 days. Adjunctive dexamethasone recommended in high-income settings. Repeat LP indicated if no clinical improvement at 48 hours.

output.summary: Empiric antibiotic regimens for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults typically combine a third-generation cephalosporin with vancomycin; ampicillin is added when Listeria coverage is indicated (age >50 or immunocompromise). Adjunctive dexamethasone has been shown in randomized controlled trials to reduce mortality and unfavorable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis when administered before or with the first dose of antibiotics (de Gans et al., NEJM 2002). Standard treatment duration for pneumococcal meningitis is 10–14 days per current guidelines. Repeat lumbar puncture is indicated for failure to improve clinically at 48 hours.

useless_tools.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis.
No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture whenever any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal neurological deficit, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60). LP performed in undetected mass effect can precipitate fatal herniation.

Blood cultures must be drawn (under interpret_labs) before the first dose of empiric antibiotics so that culture yield is not lost; in practice this means peripheral cultures are collected at the same draw as the CSF analysis is initiated, and the lab tube sequencing prevents antibiotic exposure before specimen acquisition.

critical_actions: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
key_reasoning_points: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect workup toward primary endocrine or volume-status causes of hyponatremia.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: SIADH is a common complication OF bacterial meningitis itself; treat with fluid restriction while addressing the underlying CNS infection — do not let it distract from the meningitis diagnosis.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward - classic presentation with acute onset severe headache, high fever, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, and altered mental status with positive meningeal signs and diagnostic CSF findings
clinical_pearls: The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status is present in only about 44% of bacterial meningitis cases, but at least two of the four symptoms (headache, fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status) are present in 95%
Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults, followed by Neisseria meningitidis
Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in pneumococcal meningitis from approximately 34% to 14% when given before or with the first dose of antibiotics
A CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 has a sensitivity of 80% and specificity of 98% for bacterial meningitis
